title: NURS 1021 Unit 1 Case Study 10
description: Newborn with Rh(D) hemolytic disease (mother sensitized after her first birth without Rho(D) immune globulin): early jaundice, anemia, rising bilirubin, phototherapy, signs of bilirubin encephalopathy, exchange transfusion and prevention.

authorReview.note: New case written by Claude on 25 Nov 2026 (NURS 1021 Unit 1, batch 3); checked against Merck Manual Professional (Hemolytic Disease of the Fetus and Neonate, Apr 2024; Neonatal Hyperbilirubinemia, Nov 2026). Please review: newborn reference ranges (hemoglobin 140–220 g/L, reticulocytes 3%–7%, glucose ≥ 2.6 mmol/L, vital signs); bilirubin values against the hour-specific phototherapy/exchange chart your program uses (no thresholds are quoted in the case); phototherapy nursing points (standard practice); this is a maternal-newborn topic within a med-surg unit.

question.explanation:
Require follow-up: jaundice that appears in the first 24 hours is pathologic until proven otherwise; physiologic jaundice appears after the first day. Here maternal antibodies are destroying the newborn's red cells (hemolysis), releasing unconjugated bilirubin faster than the immature liver can conjugate it. Pallor reflects anemia from hemolysis. The liver and spleen enlarge as they remove damaged cells and make new ones (extramedullary hematopoiesis). Sleepiness, poor feeding and a weak suck can be early signs of bilirubin affecting the brain (acute bilirubin encephalopathy) and need urgent assessment.

Expected newborn findings: bluish hands and feet with a pink trunk (acrocyanosis) in the first day, erythema toxicum (white papules on a red base), congenital dermal melanocytosis over the lower back, and molding of the head after vaginal birth.

History: an Rh-negative mother, an Rh-positive father, no Rho(D) immune globulin after the first birth and an anti-D titer of 1:64 (critical titers are usually 1:8 to 1:32) explain the findings.

question.stem: For each finding, click to specify whether it is expected for a healthy newborn or supports hemolytic disease of the newborn.

columns: Supports Hemolytic Disease of the Newborn

rows.text: Total bilirubin 176 µmol/L at 10 hours of age

question.explanation:
Pathogenesis (answering the client): during the first delivery, some of the first child's Rh-positive red cells entered the client's circulation. The client's immune system made anti-D antibodies; the first child was born before that response developed and was not affected. In this pregnancy, the client's IgG anti-D crossed the placenta, coated the newborn's Rh-positive red cells and caused their destruction. A dose of Rho(D) immune globulin within 72 hours of the first birth would most likely have prevented the sensitization.

Supports hemolytic disease: a positive DAT shows maternal antibody on the newborn's red cells. Hemoglobin of 118 g/L is low for a newborn (anemia from hemolysis), and 14% reticulocytes show the marrow trying to replace the cells. A total bilirubin of 176 µmol/L at 10 hours is far above expected for that age and, with a known hemolytic cause, is above the phototherapy threshold.

Expected: direct bilirubin is normal: the problem is overproduction of unconjugated bilirubin, not liver or bile duct disease. Glucose is normal.

question.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

cloze.text: The newborn's bilirubin rose by about [[drop0]] over 6 hours, which shows [[drop1]]. The nurse's priority is preventing [[drop2]].

options.text: an obstruction of the bile ducts

question.explanation:
Rate of rise: 176 to 224 µmol/L in 6 hours is 48 µmol/L, or 8 µmol/L per hour. A rise faster than about 5 µmol/L per hour in the first 24 hours is a red flag for hemolysis.

Meaning: physiologic jaundice begins after 24 hours and rises slowly; breastfeeding jaundice appears in the first week with poor intake (this newborn is formula-fed); bile duct obstruction raises conjugated bilirubin, which is normal here.

Priority: unconjugated bilirubin is fat-soluble; when it exceeds the binding capacity of albumin it crosses the blood-brain barrier and deposits in the basal ganglia and brainstem. Early signs are lethargy and poor feeding, progressing to high-pitched cry, hypotonia then hypertonia and arching, seizures and permanent damage (kernicterus: cerebral palsy, hearing loss). Late-preterm birth (37 weeks) and hemolysis increase the risk.

question.stem: Which interventions should the nurse include in the newborn's plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Give glucose water between feeds to flush out the bilirubin
Check the newborn's temperature at least every 3 to 4 hours
Protect each bilirubin sample from light
Cover the newborn's eyes with eye shields while the lights are on
Apply lotion to the skin to prevent drying under the lights
Feed every 3 hours and record wet diapers and stools
Undress the newborn except for a diaper to expose as much skin as possible
Judge the response by how yellow the newborn's skin looks

question.explanation:
Include: blue-green light changes bilirubin in the skin into water-soluble forms excreted in bile and urine without conjugation. Eyes are shielded to protect the retina (Option 4). Maximal skin exposure increases the dose of light (Option 7). Phototherapy can cause overheating or heat loss, so temperature is monitored (Option 2). Feeding promotes stooling (bilirubin leaves in stool) and replaces increased insensible water loss; loose green stools are expected (Option 6). Bilirubin breaks down in light, so samples are shielded to avoid falsely low results (Option 3).

Do not include: lotions and oils can cause burns under the lights (Option 5). Water or dextrose does not lower bilirubin and displaces milk, which is needed for stooling (Option 1). Phototherapy bleaches the skin while serum bilirubin can remain high, so the response is judged by serum bilirubin, not skin color (Option 8).

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 2 0700, the Vital Signs, and the Laboratory Results.
question.stem: For each nursing action, click to specify whether the action is Indicated, Non-Essential, or Contraindicated while the exchange transfusion is prepared.

rows.text: Continue intensive phototherapy until the exchange transfusion begins
Turn off the phototherapy to observe the newborn's skin color
Report the high-pitched cry and difficulty rousing to the neonatologist at once
Place the newborn on a cardiorespiratory monitor and maintain warmth under a radiant warmer
Give the newborn Rho(D) immune globulin
Repeat the direct antiglobulin test before the exchange

question.explanation:
Indicated: phototherapy continues to lower bilirubin while blood is prepared. A high-pitched cry, poor suck and difficulty rousing are signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy: urgent exchange transfusion can prevent permanent damage. An exchange transfusion replaces about twice the newborn's blood volume in small aliquots, removing bilirubin and antibody-coated cells and correcting anemia; heart rate, breathing, temperature, glucose and calcium are monitored closely.

Contraindicated: stopping phototherapy lets bilirubin rise further; skin color does not reflect serum bilirubin. Rho(D) immune globulin is given to Rh-negative mothers to prevent sensitization; it is never given to an Rh-positive newborn, whose red cells it would destroy.

Non-Essential: the DAT is already positive and will not change management.

question.stem: For each statement the client makes, click to specify whether it shows that the teaching was understood or that the client needs further teaching.

rows.text: “Rho(D) immune globulin won't help me now, because I already have the antibodies.”
“In my next pregnancy, I'll have antibody tests and ultrasounds to check the baby for anemia.”
“Our next baby will be fine, because the problem came from this pregnancy.”
“The baby needs blood tests over the next few weeks, because he can still become anemic.”
“If my baby turns yellow again, we'll just put him in the sunlight at home.”
“My sister is Rh-negative too, so she should ask about the immune globulin in her pregnancy.”

question.explanation:
Understood: Rho(D) immune globulin prevents sensitization (given at 28 weeks and within 72 hours after the birth of an Rh-positive newborn, and after bleeding, trauma, amniocentesis, miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy); once antibodies exist, it cannot remove them. In later pregnancies the antibody titer is followed and, above the critical titer, middle cerebral artery Doppler ultrasound detects fetal anemia, which can be treated with intrauterine transfusion. Maternal antibodies keep destroying the newborn's cells for weeks, so late anemia is watched for. An unsensitized Rh-negative relative benefits from prophylaxis.

Needs further teaching: sensitization is permanent and the disease usually becomes more severe with each Rh-positive pregnancy. Sunlight is not a safe or measurable treatment and can burn or overheat a newborn; returning jaundice, poor feeding or sleepiness need prompt assessment.
